title: Import CSV and text with confidence
goal: Choose explicit parsing rules, preserve identifiers, and verify imported records.
prerequisites: You can inspect a DataFrame, identify missing values, and read a CSV file.

cells.title: Inspect a real CSV before analyzing it
cells.explanation: The bundled Palmer Penguins CSV is a real public dataset, preserved from its authoritative upstream source. Read the field definitions in data/public/README.md before interpreting its values. The simplified table records 344 observations, eight fields, and source missing values written as NA.
cells.code:
path = DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(path, na_values=["NA"])
result = df.head(5)
print(result)
print("Shape:", df.shape)
print("Columns:", df.columns.tolist())
print("Missing values:")
print(df.isna().sum())

questions.prompt: What does one row describe, according to the source documentation?
questions.answer: One observed penguin in this simplified research dataset. The table does not provide an animal ID.

questions.prompt: Will the preview contain only complete observations?
questions.answer: No. The fourth source record lacks its measurements and sex, so missing values are visible in the first five rows.

questions.prompt: Why does a successful read_csv call not prove the data are ready for every analysis?
questions.answer: You still need to check field meaning, units, types, missingness, and which records the question requires.

cells.task: Read only species, island, and body_mass_g using usecols. Store the full three-column table in result and print its shape and the number of known body masses.
cells.hint: Pass the three names as a list to usecols; count() counts known values.
cells.solution:
path = DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.csv"
result = pd.read_csv(path, usecols=["species", "island", "body_mass_g"], na_values=["NA"])
print(result.head())
print("Shape:", result.shape)
print("Known body masses:", result["body_mass_g"].count())
cells.solution_note: The result has 344 rows and three columns. There are 342 known body masses; two missing measurements remain missing.

check.prompt: How many body masses support a summary of the available measurements?
check.feedback: Two of the 344 body-mass entries are missing. The 333 complete-record count answers a different question.

cells.verify:
assert df.shape == (344, 8)
assert result.shape == (5, 8)
assert pd.isna(result.loc[3, "body_mass_g"])
assert df["body_mass_g"].count() == 342
cells.solution_verify:
assert result.shape == (344, 3)
assert result.columns.tolist() == ["species", "island", "body_mass_g"]
assert result["body_mass_g"].count() == 342
cells.watch: These are historical study observations from 2007–2009, not current measurements or a population census.
cells.takeaway: Inspect the parsed table and its documentation together.

cells.title: The separator is part of the file contract
cells.explanation: A text file does not need a .csv extension to hold a table. Its delimiter determines where fields begin and end. The TSV and TXT files here are documented format conversions of the same public observations, so you can compare the imports directly.
cells.code:
path = DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.tsv"
wrong = pd.read_csv(path, sep=",")
result = pd.read_csv(path, sep="\t", na_values=["NA"])
print("With a comma separator:", wrong.shape)
print("With a tab separator:", result.shape)
print(result.head(3))

questions.prompt: Why does the comma-based import have only one column?
questions.answer: The TSV uses tabs between fields; a comma separator does not split those fields.

questions.prompt: What shape should the correctly parsed TSV have?
questions.answer: 344 rows and eight columns, matching the original CSV.

questions.prompt: Does changing a filename extension change its internal delimiter?
questions.answer: No. Parsing must follow the actual file contents and documented format.

cells.task: Read penguins.txt into result using its semicolon separator and skip its two comment lines using comment="#". Read penguins.csv into reference and compare the two parsed tables.
cells.hint: Use pd.read_csv even though the extension is .txt.
cells.solution:
folder = DATA_DIR / "public"
result = pd.read_csv(folder / "penguins.txt", sep=";", comment="#", encoding="utf-8", na_values=["NA"])
reference = pd.read_csv(folder / "penguins.csv", na_values=["NA"])
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, reference)
print(result.head(3))
print("Same parsed values, columns, and row order as the source CSV.")
cells.solution_note: The comment lines are excluded from the table, and all 344 observations remain. No conversion to an Excel file is necessary to read this text format.

check.prompt: Which setting separates a TSV into fields?
check.feedback: TSV means tab-separated values, so the delimiter is a tab.

cells.verify:
assert wrong.shape == (344, 1)
assert result.shape == (344, 8)
assert result.loc[0, "bill_length_mm"] == 39.1
cells.watch: Do not use skiprows to hide unexpected malformed records; first identify what those rows mean.
cells.takeaway: Read a table according to its actual delimiter and header rules.

cells.title: Preserve leading zeros and literal NA codes
cells.explanation: This small import fixture is explicitly fictional and separate from the penguin research data. Its IDs contain leading zeros, NA is a literal site code, and MISSING marks one unavailable amount. Encoding, quoting, decimal symbols, and missing-value rules all affect what a reader produces.
cells.code:
path = DATA_DIR / "public" / "import_practice_semicolon.csv"
result = pd.read_csv(path, sep=";", comment="#", encoding="utf-8-sig", dtype="string", keep_default_na=False)
print(result)
print("IDs:", result["record_id"].tolist())
print("Site codes:", result["site_code"].tolist())

questions.prompt: Why is record_id read as text?
questions.answer: It is an identifier, not a quantity. Converting 001 to an integer would lose its leading zeros.

questions.prompt: Does the NA site code become a missing value in this import?
questions.answer: No. keep_default_na=False preserves the literal code as text.

questions.prompt: Why does the semicolon inside the second note not create an extra column?
questions.answer: The field is quoted using CSV quoting rules, so the embedded separator belongs to the note.

cells.task: Read the fixture again with record_id and site_code as strings, comma decimal symbols for amount_eur, and only MISSING in amount_eur treated as missing. Keep the NA site code unchanged. Print the known amount count and sum.
cells.hint: Use decimal="," and a column-specific na_values dictionary while keeping keep_default_na=False.
cells.solution:
path = DATA_DIR / "public" / "import_practice_semicolon.csv"
result = pd.read_csv(path, sep=";", comment="#", encoding="utf-8-sig", dtype={"record_id": "string", "site_code": "string"}, decimal=",", keep_default_na=False, na_values={"amount_eur": ["MISSING"]})
print(result)
print("Known amounts:", result["amount_eur"].count())
print("Known amount sum:", result["amount_eur"].sum())
cells.solution_note: The amounts are 12.5, missing, and 0.0 EUR. Two known amounts sum to 12.5; the missing value was not replaced with zero. Both NA site codes and all leading-zero IDs are preserved.

check.prompt: Which is a safe way to preserve leading-zero identifiers?
options: Read the identifier column with dtype="string"
check.feedback: Identifiers need their full text representation even when they contain only digits.

cells.verify:
assert result.shape == (3, 4)
assert result["record_id"].tolist() == ["001", "010", "100"]
assert result["site_code"].tolist() == ["NA", "EU", "NA"]
assert result.loc[1, "note"] == "quoted; semicolon"
cells.solution_verify:
assert result["record_id"].tolist() == ["001", "010", "100"]
assert result["site_code"].tolist() == ["NA", "EU", "NA"]
assert result["amount_eur"].count() == 2
assert result["amount_eur"].sum() == 12.5
assert result.loc[2, "amount_eur"] == 0.0
cells.watch: The meanings NA=North Area and EU=East Unit apply only to this invented fixture. Do not impose those meanings on other sources.
cells.takeaway: Specify identifiers, missing tokens, and number formats deliberately.

cells.title: Verify a CSV round trip with explicit types
cells.explanation: A CSV stores text and does not carry a pandas dtype schema. A repeatable import can specify its expected text, integer, and measurement types. Exporting and reading back the table lets you check that values, missingness, and the chosen schema survive.
cells.code:
schema = {"species": "string", "island": "string", "bill_length_mm": "Float64", "bill_depth_mm": "Float64", "flipper_length_mm": "Int64", "body_mass_g": "Int64", "sex": "string", "year": "Int64"}
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.csv", dtype=schema, na_values=["NA"])
path = OUTPUT_DIR / "penguins_round_trip.csv"
df.to_csv(path, index=False, na_rep="NA")
result = pd.read_csv(path, dtype=schema, na_values=["NA"])
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, df)
print("Rows and columns:", result.shape)
print(result.dtypes)
print("Round-trip values and declared types match.")

questions.prompt: Why use nullable Int64 for body_mass_g?
questions.answer: The source contains whole-number masses and missing entries; nullable Int64 represents both without inventing values.

questions.prompt: How many columns should the exported CSV contain?
questions.answer: Eight, because index=False does not add the DataFrame index as a ninth field.

questions.prompt: Why specify the schema again when reading the exported CSV?
questions.answer: CSV has no embedded pandas dtype contract, so the reader would otherwise infer types again.

cells.task: Using the same explicit schema, store only Gentoo observations in gentoo with a reset index. Export gentoo to penguins_gentoo.csv, read the file back into result, and compare result with gentoo.
cells.hint: Reset the filtered index because the CSV intentionally does not store it.
cells.solution:
schema = {"species": "string", "island": "string", "bill_length_mm": "Float64", "bill_depth_mm": "Float64", "flipper_length_mm": "Int64", "body_mass_g": "Int64", "sex": "string", "year": "Int64"}
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.csv", dtype=schema, na_values=["NA"])
gentoo = df.loc[df["species"] == "Gentoo"].reset_index(drop=True)
path = OUTPUT_DIR / "penguins_gentoo.csv"
gentoo.to_csv(path, index=False, na_rep="NA")
result = pd.read_csv(path, dtype=schema, na_values=["NA"])
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, gentoo)
print("Gentoo rows:", len(result))
print("Known body masses:", result["body_mass_g"].count())
cells.solution_note: The subset contains 124 Gentoo observations, with 123 known body masses. Its row labels are newly created positions, not animal identities.

check.prompt: Does a CSV automatically preserve a pandas nullable-integer dtype?
options: Yes, every dtype is stored inside CSV
No; provide the intended dtype when importing
Only if the filename contains Int64
check.feedback: CSV stores fields as text; the receiving reader applies the type rules.

cells.verify:
assert result.shape == (344, 8)
assert str(result["body_mass_g"].dtype) == "Int64"
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, df)
cells.solution_verify:
assert result.shape == (124, 8)
assert result["body_mass_g"].count() == 123
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, gentoo)
cells.watch: An export should go to OUTPUT_DIR, leaving the downloaded source unchanged.
cells.takeaway: Treat an import/export schema as part of reproducibility.
